issue.issue_text: Whether the Writ Petitions should be allowed.

facts: A batch of writ petitions was filed seeking a declaration to permit the live streaming of Supreme Court case proceedings.
The petitioners specifically requested live streaming for cases of constitutional and national importance, arguing it would enhance public access to justice and uphold the citizens' right to know.
application: The Supreme Court considered the arguments presented by the petitioners and the Attorney General for India.
The central argument was that live dissemination of court proceedings using technology would allow litigants and the wider society to have greater access to and understanding of judicial proceedings.
In anticipation of granting the relief sought, the Court requested the Attorney General to collate suggestions and help evolve a framework and guidelines for implementing live streaming.
The Court also established that it would retain the power to grant, refuse, or revoke permission for live streaming in any case to ensure that the administration of justice is not compromised.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court allowed the writ petitions, thereby accepting the plea to permit the live streaming of its proceedings, particularly in cases of constitutional and national importance, and began the process of creating a framework for its implementation.

obiter: Article 145 (1) of the Constitution provides that subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the Supreme Court may from time to time, with the approval of the President, make rules for regulating generally the practice and procedure of the Court.
These regulations are rules are silent on taking consent from parties involved the matter.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that the petitions, brought in the larger public interest, should be accepted to uphold the constitutional rights of the public and litigants. It recognized that court proceedings ought to be live-streamed, based on the principle of open justice, while balancing this against other interests such as the dignity and privacy of participants, the majesty and decorum of the Courts, and the overall administration of justice.
legal_tests_applied: A balancing test where the principle of open justice is weighed against the paramount object of the administration of justice. Open justice must yield if it becomes necessary to restrict access in the facts of a particular case, such as when excessive publicity itself operates as an instrument of injustice.

A discretionary test for granting or refusing permission for live streaming, guided by considerations such as: (a) the unanimous consent of the parties, (b) the sensitivity of the subject matter, including cases that may arouse passion or social unrest, and (c) any other reason in the larger interest of justice, including whether the broadcast would affect the dignity of the court or prejudice the right to a fair trial.
why_respondent_won: The principle of open justice is a long-established and central aspect of the fair administration of justice and the rule of law, encompassing the public's right to attend court, receive fair reports of proceedings, and access reasoned judgments.

Hearing cases in open court is of the utmost importance for maintaining public confidence in the impartial administration of justice, as it ensures that justice is not only done but is also seen to be done.
Openness operates as a wholesome check upon judicial behaviour and the conduct of the contending parties and their witnesses, thereby preventing judicial improbity and ensuring accountability.
The cause was brought in the larger public interest and its acceptance upholds the constitutional rights of the public and litigants to access justice.
policy_considerations: Public confidence in the administration of justice is of such great significance that courts must generally hear causes in open and permit public admission to the court-room.
An objective of the judicial power is the satisfaction of the parties and the general public that, through open procedures, justice has both been done and been seen to be done.

While open justice is the default, it must yield to the paramount object of the administration of justice. If excessive publicity operates as an instrument of injustice, the court may impose necessary restraints to secure its primary object.
The court must retain the power to revoke permission for live streaming at any stage if the situation warrants, ensuring that the cause of administration of justice does not suffer.
